Hey, you! Glad you're here. Let me introduce myself: I am Nurdoidz, the creator of the LifeNotes system. I've maintained this system for a few years, but still can say that great improvements are possible. Oh, dear me. You probably don't know what I'm yammering about. Let me brief you:

LifeNotes is an indexed journaling system based around tags and an index to organize notes or entries of all types to be easily referenced in the future.

LifeNotes is a solution to a problem I had. See, I am not the kind of guy who finds writing long entries about daily life exhilarating. Nor do I enjoy trying to find which entry had which event in a regular journal. Sure, there's a lot of software I can buy to organize my entries well, but almost all of them rely on their own proprietary formats. I wanted something that:

  • uses tags that can be searched to find items or events easily
  • does not restrict you to any page size; can be short or long
  • uses no extra software than what comes with every computer OS
  • cross-platform
  • can be used to notetake, keep a diary, make a scrapbook, or just write

I scoured the Internet and found nothing. People just weren't passionate about organized journaling as I was. So, there came a point along this history flashback that I realized that no one else was going to do it but me. Thus, LifeNotes was born.

How it Works

LifeNotes is too good for special software or proprietary formats. LifeNotes was built to be versatile, out-of-the-way, and useful. The only thing you need is a word processor. That's right: even smartphones can use the LifeNotes system (results may vary). After all, I write 20% of my lifenotes on my phone.

Let's dive into the hardware that powers LifeNotes.

Lifenotes

The lifenotes are the actual entries in your journal. They can be about anything. Heck, they don't even need to be text-based. You can go so far and say that LifeNotes can be used as a scrapbook. It can be daily diary entries, pictures of the tickets you got for a concert, or even a basic note you jotted down about some song you heard on the radio.

Tags

All lifenotes have tags. Tags are the most important part in order for the system to work. They're basically labels or keywords that describe the content in the lifenote. Tags are the handles used by the index for future research when you come back.

Index

The lifenotes, which are handled by their tags, are all organized in the index. The index is the spine of the system, connecting all of the notes, by their tags, into one central place. When you go back to read a lifenote, the index is the first stop you'll make.

Getting Started

Now that you've sampled the mashed potatoes of this thanksgiving dinner, it's time to jump on the framework, the tools. The first thing you're going to need are the templates.

Templates are the files that're going to make your life easier and make your journal look more consistent when you use LifeNotes. The templates I made currently exist in two formats: Microsoft Office Open XML (*.dotx) and OpenDocument (*.ott). Here are the files:

  • Index Template: Template-index.dotx | Template-index.ott
  • Lifenote Template: Template-lifenote.dotx | Template-lifenote.ott

I've slaved over the workstation, locked inside the dungeon, forging the templates and system to make creating lifenotes an easy and painless task. First, we're going to create a new document using the Template-lifenote file you downloaded earlier (Figure 1). The only thing you should see is a whole bunch of nothing with a line saying 'tags' at the bottom. The blinking cursor should be at the top-center of the page.

The blank space is actually three sections of the lifenote (Figure 2). The cursor starts at the date position, since that's the first thing you're going to write. Then, when you press down, on the next line, is the title. That, if you haven't guessed already, is your lifenote title, if you want one. The line below that is your actual entry text. Finally, below the entry, is the tags section.

Date

You can use whatever format you want for the date. If you want to be cool like me, though, the format I always use is:

Tuesday, 18 November 2014 at 15:16

Be sure to include the year, month, and day so it's handy when naming the file later. It's like going hunting without a gun.

Note: The date is specially formatted to be all-caps.

Title

The title, if used, will appear in the file name. There is no standard format for the title, so name your lifenotes whatever you'd like.

Entry

This is where your actual entry will live. Write as much as you like or add some pictures instead if you'd like. I've crafted a few formatting options to use as nifty extras:

  • Headings: headings 1, 2, and 3 have been adjusted to fit the theme. Feel free to use them for extra-long lifenotes!
  • Quote: a shaded block quote to emphasize dialog, quotes, or something someone said on the Internet.
  • Code: though not something most people would use, a shaded block of code for use with source code, ASCII art, or whatever else you can do with fixed-width text.

Tags

This is the most important part needed for the LifeNotes system to work. If you've ever published a blog, this is pretty straightforward. But, as I know myself, tags are sometimes hard to think of and sometimes you'll be tempted to just skip it.

Tags are basically keywords that describe your entry. For example, the following can be considered keywords:

  • a song
  • a place
  • a person
  • a topic

You can think of it this way, when you take a nostalgia trip back to the past in your journal, what do you think you'd search for in the index?

Tags are usually separated by commas, but it would be wrong of me to say that's the only way.

You can basically use any organization strategy you choose for LifeNotes (as long as you can index it easily), but, if you feel like going pro and follow my way, I'll explain.

File Organization

My entire directory of lifenotes is stored in one folder I call LifeNotes. Yes, this folder is portable, so you can store it on a flash drive or something. Inside this folder, I have:

  • my templates.
  • my unfiled lifenotes.
  • file folders for each lifetab.

A lifetab is a section inside LifeNotes that depicts a big category in your journal. You can have a section for general life, one for cool pictures, one for frustrations and rants, and even one for short stories or something. Each lifetab is assigned a 1-digit ID number, starting at 0 (or 1 if you choose). For example, here is how my LifeNotes root folder looks:

0-Life (File folder)
1-Work (File folder)
2-Poetry (File folder)
3-Rants (File folder)
4-Love (File folder)
Word-count.xlsx (Excel worksheet)
LifeNotes-index.docx (Word document)
Template-index.dotx (Word template)
Template-lifenote.dotx (Word template)
Template-index.ott (ODF template)
Template-lifenote.ott (ODF template)

Therefore, my poetry lifetab would be assigned a '2'.

Note: For those who fear numbers, fret not; they are a guide for you later when you index. You'll eventually learn how to quickly read these numbers and it'll become second-nature. No math involved, I promise.

Let's go inside one of my lifetab folders, say, Life:

2012-09-September (File folder)
2012-10-October (File folder)
2013-01-January (File folder)
2013-13-MysteryMonth (File folder)
2014-04-April (File folder)
2014-05-May (File folder)

As you can see, they are sorted first by year (2012, 2013, 2014), then by month (9 for September, 10 for October, 1 for January, and so on). Adding the month names after is completely optional. I do it because it's faster to read sometimes.

Then, inside one of these folders, 2014-15-May:

01-1-Not-Really-Proud-of-Myself.docx (Word document)
05-1-Cinco-de-Mayo.docx (Word document)
05-2-A-Green-Tree.docx (Word document)
19-1-An Exciting Day to Add.docx (Word document)
21-1-I-Always-Forget-Something.docx (Word document)

Yes, these are my actual entry names. Anyway, in this folder, it is first sorted by day (1, 5, 19, 21), then by what I call a cumulative lifenote ID. This is an ID that's assigned to each lifenote based on how it ranks against others that also fall in the same day.

The first lifenote of the day gets a '1'. Then, if another note is made in the same day afterwards, it is assigned a '2', then a '3', and so on. It accumulates.

After the CLID, the title is added. So, just by file and folder names, we have the following information about each entry:

  • the year
  • the month
  • the day
  • which order it was made in that day
  • the title

With this information, we can then assign a lifenote ID to each lifenote for future reference in the index. You can think of it like being a page number in a regular text book or a unique URL to a specific video. A lifenote ID takes the following format:

T-YY-MM-DD-C

An example lifenote ID would look as follows:

2-2013-06-05-3

This ID can be divided in the following way:

  • T: the lifetab it falls under
  • YYYY: the year
  • MM: the month
  • DD: the day
  • C: the cumulative lifenote ID

So with the lifenote ID 2-2013-06-05-3, we can say that it is a poem written on 5 June 2013, which was the third poem written that day.

Note: Keep in mind that this is purposely named a 'guide' so you can take these ideas and form them to fit your style. After all, journals are about you.

Save Location

Generally, a lifenote I save before I index it is considered unfiled. An unfiled lifenote is usually saved in the root directory of the LifeNotes folder. After a certain time you please, you will then file and index all of your entries (or you can do it right away).

This is the bulk of the work you're going to do on your journal, but it'll be worth it when you want to research your lifenotes later on. The index is where all of your tags from your lifenotes will be compiled to be referenced for later on. I have one massive index, but you can have as many as you please, even one for each lifetab or so.

The first thing you're going to do is create an index.

Creating an Index

Create a new document from the Template-index template file you downloaded earlier. Inside you will see a few example sections and tags and the like to give you an idea of how the index is organized.

Basically, there are categories. Examples: People, Music, Keywords, etc.
Inside each category, there are index letters to sort your tags alphabetically.
Inside each index letter, there are keywords, or tags. These are your actual tags.
Inside each keyword, there are references to entries. These are the lifenote ID's we discussed earlier. They point you to which entry had which tag.

In your word processor, each style (category, index letter, keyword, entry) is already designed to allow easy additions. They are already indented and formatted. In fact, I made it so that after going to the next line after category, the index letter will automatically be selected. After the index letter, the keyword would be selected automatically, and so on.

After you enter a lifenote ID under each tag (note that you can add multiple IDs under one tag), you can press Tab to add an explanation in case you'd like to make research easier later on. The template already has a few examples you can look over.

Indexing a Lifenote

Now that the hard part is done, you can start indexing and filing your entries. After I index my tags, I usually file my lifenote in its appropriate folder. So, basically, here is the entire process of the LifeNotes system:

  1. Create a few lifenotes and place them in the LifeNotes root folder.
  2. Create an index and place it in the LifeNotes root folder (or in each lifetab folder if you wish).
  3. Index the tags of one of the lifenotes.
  4. File that lifenote in its appropriate folder.
  5. Repeat #3-4 until all lifenotes are filed.
  6. Create more lifenotes.
  7. Repeat #3-6.
